problems.title: Problem 1
problems.problem:
Problem 1

The height of a certain coal mine in Datong, Shanxi, relative to Qinhuangdao is $h_{\mathrm{c}}$. A train of mass $m_{\mathrm{t}}$ carrying coal of mass $m_{\mathrm{c}}$ travels from Datong along the Daqin railway a distance $l$ and arrives at Qinhuangdao; after unloading, the empty train returns. On the way from Datong to Qinhuangdao, part of the total potential energy of the train and the coal is used to do work against the resistance of the rails and the air, and the remaining part is converted into electrical energy by a generator, with average conversion efficiency $\eta_1$; the electrical energy is entirely stored in a storage battery for use on the return trip. On the return trip the empty train is driven by an electric motor powered by the stored electrical energy, doing work against gravity and resistance; the average efficiency of converting the stored electrical energy into external work is $\eta_2$. Assume that the work the train must do against resistance per unit distance travelled on the Daqin line is, on average, proportional to the total weight (of the train, or of the train and the coal) while running, the proportionality coefficient being the constant $\mu$. The train carries no electrical energy when it departs from Datong.

(1) If there is still electrical energy left when the empty train has returned to Datong, find this energy $E$.

(2) What is the minimum mass of coal the train must carry so that it can just return to Datong without any additional energy being supplied?

(3) Given that the average speed of the train on the railway from Datong to Qinhuangdao is $v$, give the relation between the average output power $P$ of the generator and the other physical quantities given in the problem.

Physical constants and formulas that may be used (printed at the beginning of the paper): speed of light in vacuum $c=2.998\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m/s}$; the magnitude of the gravitational acceleration at the Earth's surface is $g$; Planck's constant is $h$, $\hbar=\dfrac{h}{2\pi}$; $\displaystyle\int\frac{1}{1-x^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\ln\frac{1+x}{1-x}+C,\quad |x|<1$.

problems.title: Problem 3
problems.problem:
Problem 3 [15 points]

The Martian atmosphere may be regarded as consisting only of very thin $\mathrm{CO_2}$, whose molar mass is denoted by $\mu$; the atmosphere at a given height may be regarded as an ideal gas in equilibrium. The mass of Mars is $M_{\mathrm{m}}$ (much larger than the total mass of the Martian atmosphere) and its radius is $R_{\mathrm{m}}$. Assume that the mass density of the Martian atmosphere depends on the height $h$ above the Martian surface as

$$\rho(h)=\rho_0\left(1+\frac{h}{R_{\mathrm{m}}}\right)^{1-n},$$

where $\rho_0$ is a constant and $n$ ($n>4$) is a constant.

(1) Find the expression for the temperature of the Martian atmosphere as a function of the height $h$.

(2) To explore the Martian surface, a lander of mass $m_{\mathrm{t}}$ and of rather high mass density is to be released onto the Martian surface. The lander is released from rest at a certain height much smaller than $R_{\mathrm{m}}$, and after a time $t_i$ it lands on the Martian surface. During the descent the lander does not rotate, and the gravitational acceleration of Mars and the atmospheric density may both be taken equal to their values at the Martian surface. When the descent speed of the lander is $v$, the atmospheric drag on it is proportional to the product of the atmospheric density and $v^2$, the proportionality coefficient being the constant $k$. Find the speed of the lander just before landing.

Physical constants and formulas that may be used (printed at the beginning of the paper): speed of light in vacuum $c=2.998\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m/s}$; the magnitude of the gravitational acceleration at the Earth's surface is $g$; Planck's constant is $h$, $\hbar=\dfrac{h}{2\pi}$; $\displaystyle\int\frac{1}{1-x^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\ln\frac{1+x}{1-x}+C,\quad |x|<1$.

problems.title: Problem 4
problems.problem:
Problem 4

Photons, which carry a certain energy and momentum, also carry angular momentum. The angular momentum of a photon of circularly polarized light has magnitude $\hbar$. When a photon is absorbed by an object, the energy, momentum and angular momentum of the photon are all transferred to the object. The angular momentum acquired by an object from absorbed photons can make the object rotate. Using this principle, under continuous irradiation by circularly polarized laser light, scientists have achieved high-speed rotation of nanoparticles, obtaining the fastest micro-scale rotor in a liquid environment so far.

As shown in the figure, a gold nanosphere is placed between two horizontal smooth glass plates, and the whole (including the glass plates) is immersed in water. A beam of circularly polarized laser light shines from above downwards onto the gold nanosphere. The wavelength of this incident laser light in vacuum is $\lambda=830\ \mathrm{nm}$; after being focused by a microscope objective (it is still assumed to be a plane wave, each photon having angular momentum $\hbar$ along the direction of propagation), the diameter of the light spot is $d=1.20\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m}$ and the power is $P=20.0\ \mathrm{mW}$. The radius of the gold nanosphere is $R=100\ \mathrm{nm}$, and the density of gold is $\rho=19.32\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{kg/m^{3}}$. Neglecting the reflection of light at the interfaces between media and losses such as the absorption of light by the glass and the water, and considering only the rotation of the gold nanosphere driven by the angular momentum it acquires by absorbing photons, analyse the following questions (give the computed results to 3 significant figures):

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/cpho-2016-1-4-fig1.png

[圆偏振激光 = circularly polarized laser light; 玻璃 = glass; 水 = water; 金 = gold]

(1) Find the frequency $\nu$ and the intensity $I$ (the power transmitted per unit cross-sectional area in the direction of propagation) of this laser beam.

(2) Give the values of the mass $m$ of the gold nanosphere and of its moment of inertia $J$ about its axis of symmetry.

(3) Assuming that the absorption cross-section of the particle for the light (the ratio of the light power absorbed by the particle to the incident light intensity) is $\sigma_{\mathrm{abs}}=0.123\,\pi R^{2}$, find the magnitude $M$ of the torque exerted by this laser beam on the particle about its axis of symmetry of rotation.

(4) It is known that a spherical particle (of radius $r$) rotating with angular velocity $\omega$ in a liquid of viscosity coefficient $\eta$ experiences a viscous friction torque of magnitude $M_{\mathrm{f}}=8\pi\eta r^{3}\omega$. Given that the viscosity coefficient of water is $\eta=8.00\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{Pa\cdot s}$, find the rotation rate (revolutions per second) $f$ of the gold nanosphere when it reaches steady rotation under irradiation by this beam.

(5) Taking as time zero, $t_0=0$, the instant at which the light begins to shine on the gold nanoparticle at rest, find the expression $f(t)$ for the rotation rate of the particle at an arbitrary time $t$ ($t>0$).

(6) If the incident laser beam is replaced by a square-wave pulsed laser beam with pulse width $T_1$ (during which the light intensity is still $I$) and interval between pulses $T_2$, and the instant at which the light of the first pulse begins to shine on the particle is taken as time zero, $t_0=0$, find the expression for the rotation rate $f_n$ of the particle at the instant after $n$ complete pulse periods ($T_1+T_2$), and give the expression for the limiting rotation rate $f_{n\to\infty}$.

Physical constants and formulas that may be used (printed at the beginning of the paper): speed of light in vacuum $c=2.998\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m/s}$; the magnitude of the gravitational acceleration at the Earth's surface is $g$; Planck's constant is $h$, $\hbar=\dfrac{h}{2\pi}$; $\displaystyle\int\frac{1}{1-x^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\ln\frac{1+x}{1-x}+C,\quad |x|<1$.

problems.title: Problem 5
problems.problem:
Problem 5

Many racing cars are fitted with adjustable aerofoil wings, which can provide a car on a horizontal road with an additional pressing force, vertically upwards or downwards. If the speed of the racing car is $v$, the magnitude of this force is $f_B=c_Bv^{2}$, where $c_B$ is a constant. When the front of the wing is tilted up, the force is directed upwards; when the rear of the wing is tilted up, the force is directed downwards. During its motion the racing car experiences air resistance from the oncoming air of magnitude $f_A=c_Av^{2}$, where $c_A$ is a constant. The mass of the racing car is $m$, and the coefficient of static friction between the tyres and the road is $\mu_S$ ($\mu_S<1$).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/cpho-2016-1-5-fig1.jpg

(1) The racing car travels at constant speed on a straight horizontal road. Taking into account the deformation of the tyres during the motion, the road exerts a resistance on the car whose magnitude is proportional to the magnitude of the normal force between the car and the road, with proportionality coefficient $\mu_R$ ($\mu_R<\mu_S$). If the wing is adjusted with its front tilted up, find at what speed the output power of the car's engine is maximal. What is the maximum output power?

(2) Neglecting the ground resistance caused by the deformation of the tyres during the motion, find the maximum allowed speed $v_{\max}$ when the racing car travels at constant speed along a circular road of radius $r$ on horizontal ground without sliding on the road surface or leaving the ground. In this case, should the wing be adjusted with its front tilted up or its rear tilted up so that $v_{\max}$ can be larger? Assume that the output power of the car's engine can be sufficiently large.

problems.title: Problem 6
problems.problem:
Problem 6

Hyperloop is a system that achieves ultra-high-speed transportation by means of the fast motion of capsule-shaped transport vehicles in horizontal tubes (see Fig. a). It uses the "air cushion" technique and the "linear motor" principle.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/cpho-2016-1-6-fig1.png

[图a = Fig. a]

The "air cushion" technique consists in ejecting high-pressure gas from inside the horizontally placed transport vehicle at high speed through small holes in its lower half (see Fig. b), so that the whole transport vehicle is lifted off the tube wall by a very small distance and friction can be neglected. The cross-section of the transport vehicle is a circle of radius $R$, and a large number of small radial holes are uniformly distributed over the lower half of the vehicle wall, the number of holes per unit area being $n$ ($n\gg1$) and the area of a single hole being $s$. The length of the transport vehicle is $l$ and its mass is $M$. The gas flow may be regarded as obeying Bernoulli's equation, with the temperature unchanged; the pressure of the gas at the outlets of the holes is the lower ambient pressure $P_{\mathrm{low}}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/cpho-2016-1-6-fig2.png

[运输车截面图 = cross-section of the transport vehicle; 局部放大图 = partial enlarged view; 运输车上小孔均沿径向 = the small holes in the transport vehicle are all radial; 图b = Fig. b]

As shown in Fig. c, two parallel horizontal smooth power-supply guide rails (thick solid lines) are fixed in the horizontal tube, and two conducting wires (thin solid lines) perpendicular to the rails are fixed on the transport vehicle. The cross-section of each rail is a circle of radius $r_{\mathrm{d}}$, the resistivity of the rails is $\rho_{\mathrm{d}}$, and the distance between the axes of the two rails is $2(D+r_{\mathrm{d}})$; the thickness of the two wires may be neglected and their separation is $D$; the resistance of each wire is twice the resistance of a length $D$ of rail. The two wires and the axes of the rails all lie in the same horizontal plane. The rails and the wires are in good electrical contact, and all contact resistances may be neglected.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/cpho-2016-1-6-fig3.png

[导线1 = wire 1; 导线2 = wire 2; 导轨 = guide rail; 磁场 = magnetic field; 直流电源 = DC power supply; 图c = Fig. c; 图d = Fig. d; 图e = Fig. e]

(1) Find how large the pressure of the high-pressure gas inside must be for the transport vehicle to be just lifted.

(2) As shown in Fig. d, when the transport vehicle enters a station, it slides with velocity $v_0$ along the horizontal smooth rails into a region of uniform magnetic field; the boundary of the field is parallel to the wires, the magnetic induction has magnitude $B$ and is directed perpendicularly downwards into the rail–wire plane. After both wires have entirely entered the magnetic field, find the speed with which the transport vehicle slides.

(3) When the transport vehicle is at rest on the horizontal smooth rails ready to leave the station, a constant-voltage DC power supply of electromotive force E, fixed on the rails at a distance $D$ behind wire 2, is switched on (as shown in Fig. e). The size of the power supply and the resistance of the wires connected to it may be neglected. Find the magnitude of the acceleration of the transport vehicle at the moment the power supply is switched on.

It is known that for a cylindrical straight wire segment in a closed circuit carrying a steady current, with the current uniformly distributed over the cross-section, as shown in Fig. f, the magnetic induction produced at a point at distance $r_0$ from the axis of the wire is perpendicular to the plane formed by this point and the axis of the wire, and its magnitude can be approximately calculated by

$$B=\frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi r_0}\left(\cos\theta_1+\cos\theta_2\right),$$

where $I$ is the current and $\theta_1$, $\theta_2$ are the angles between the axis of the wire and the lines joining this point to the two ends of the axis of the wire segment.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/cpho-2016-1-6-fig4.png

[图f = Fig. f]

An integral formula that may be useful:

$$\int_a^b\frac{1}{x}\,\frac{c}{\sqrt{x^{2}+c^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}x=\ln\left(\frac{b}{a}\,\frac{c+\sqrt{c^{2}+a^{2}}}{c+\sqrt{c^{2}+b^{2}}}\right),$$

where $a$, $b$, $c$ are all positive numbers.

problems.title: Problem 7
problems.problem:
Problem 7

Einstein's theory of gravitation predicts that changes in the distribution of matter cause waves in the geometric structure of spacetime: gravitational waves. For simplicity, consider a plane gravitational wave propagating along the $z$ axis. For any given $z$, the distance $\mathrm{d}r$ between two infinitely close points $(x,y)$ and $(x+\mathrm{d}x,y+\mathrm{d}y)$ in the two-dimensional $x$-$y$ space is given by

$$\mathrm{d}r=\sqrt{(1+f_1)(\mathrm{d}x)^{2}+f_2(\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}y+\mathrm{d}y\mathrm{d}x)+(1-f_1)(\mathrm{d}y)^{2}}$$

The gravitational wave manifests itself as changes (waves) of $f_1$ and $f_2$.

(1) Assume that when a plane gravitational wave passes, $f_1$ and $f_2$ can be expressed as

$$f_1=A\sin\left[\omega\left(t-\frac{z}{c}\right)\right],\quad f_2=0;\quad 0<A\ll1$$

where $A$ and $\omega$ are the amplitude and angular frequency of the wave, and $c$ is the propagation speed of the gravitational wave (equal to the speed of light).

(i) When no gravitational wave passes, in the $x$-$y$ plane, a micro-detector is placed at the origin $O$ and another at the point at distance $R$ from $O$ and at angle $\theta$ to the $x$ axis. Find the approximate expression for the deviation of the distance between the two detectors from $R$ when the gravitational wave under consideration passes.

(ii) Suppose that when no gravitational wave passes, an array of micro-detectors is placed in the $x$-$y$ plane on the circle of radius $R$ centred at the origin $O$. When the above gravitational wave is present, the spatial coordinates can be redefined as $(X,Y)$ so that the distance between two neighbouring points $(X,Y)$ and $(X+\mathrm{d}X,Y+\mathrm{d}Y)$ in the two-dimensional $X$-$Y$ space is $\sqrt{(\mathrm{d}X)^{2}+(\mathrm{d}Y)^{2}}$. Find, for a given time $t$, the shape of the distribution of the micro-detector array in the newly defined coordinate system.

(iii) If a plane gravitational wave

$$f_1=A\sin\left[\omega\left(t-\frac{z}{c}\right)\right],\quad f_2=0$$

and another plane gravitational wave

$$f_1=A\sin\left[\omega\left(t-\frac{z}{c}\right)+\phi\right],\quad f_2=0,\qquad \phi\ (0\le\phi<2\pi)\ \text{is a constant}$$

propagate simultaneously in the positive $z$ direction, what conditions must $\phi$ and $\theta$ satisfy so that the amplitude of the perturbation, caused by the gravitational waves, of the distance between the two micro-detectors placed at the origin $O$ and at the point with coordinates $(R\cos\theta,R\sin\theta)$ in the two-dimensional $x$-$y$ space reaches a maximum or a minimum?

(2) Suppose that the source of the gravitational wave is a binary star system. The two stars of the binary system each have mass $M$. Take the centre of mass of the binary system as the coordinate origin $O'$; the binary system rotates in the two-dimensional $x'$-$y'$ space. It is known that under particular conditions $f_1$ and $f_2$ can be approximately expressed as

$$f_1=\frac{8\pi G}{c^{4}}\,\frac{2}{l}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2}}{\mathrm{d}t^{2}}\left[I_1\left(t-\frac{l}{c}\right)\right],\quad f_2=\frac{8\pi G}{c^{4}}\,\frac{2}{l}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2}}{\mathrm{d}t^{2}}\left[I_2\left(t-\frac{l}{c}\right)\right]$$

where $G$ is the gravitational constant and $l$ is the distance from the gravitational-wave detection point on the $z'$ axis to the point $O'$ (much larger than the distance between the two stars of the binary system), and

$$I_1(t)=\left[x_1'^{2}(t)+x_2'^{2}(t)\right]M,\quad I_2(t)=x_1'(t)\,y_2'(t)\,M$$

$(x_1'(t),y_1'(t))$ and $(x_2'(t),y_2'(t))$ are the coordinates of the two stars in their centre-of-mass frame (note: with this definition, the coefficients in the expression for $\mathrm{d}r$ should be replaced by $f_1\to f_1$, $f_2\to 2f_2$). Given that the frequency of this gravitational wave is $\omega$, and assuming that the effect of the gravitational radiation on the orbital motion of the binary system can be neglected, find the amplitudes of $f_1$ and $f_2$ at the detection point.

Physical constants and formulas that may be used (printed at the beginning of the paper): speed of light in vacuum $c=2.998\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m/s}$; the magnitude of the gravitational acceleration at the Earth's surface is $g$; Planck's constant is $h$, $\hbar=\dfrac{h}{2\pi}$; $\displaystyle\int\frac{1}{1-x^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\ln\frac{1+x}{1-x}+C,\quad |x|<1$.

problems.title: Problem 8
problems.problem:
Problem 8

Positronium ($\mathrm{Ps}$) is a quantum bound system composed of an electron $\mathrm{e^-}$ and a positron $\mathrm{e^+}$ (the antiparticle of the electron, whose mass is the same as that of the electron and whose charge is equal in magnitude and opposite in sign to that of the electron); its energy levels can be obtained by analogy with the energy levels of the hydrogen atom. According to Bohr's theory of the hydrogen atom, the values of the angular momentum of the electron in its circular orbit around the proton are quantized, namely integer multiples of $\hbar$. Taking into account that the mass of the proton is finite, the quantization condition of the hydrogen atom should be corrected to: the total orbital angular momentum of the electron and the proton relative to their centre of mass, in the centre-of-mass frame, takes values that are integer multiples of $\hbar$. This quantization condition can be directly generalized to other two-body bound systems, such as positronium. Give all the following computed results to four significant figures.

(1) Write down the ground-state energy of positronium.

(2) The ground-state positronium atom is unstable and quickly annihilates, producing two photons:

$$\mathrm{Ps}\to\gamma_1+\gamma_2$$

When a ground-state positronium atom moving relative to the laboratory frame with a certain speed much smaller than the speed of light annihilates, one of the produced photons, $\gamma_1$, is observed in the direction at deflection angle $\theta_1$ relative to the direction of this velocity, and at the same time the other photon, $\gamma_2$, is observed in the direction at deflection angle $\Delta\theta$ ($\Delta\theta\ll1$) relative to the direction opposite to that of photon $\gamma_1$, as shown in the figure.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/cpho-2016-1-8-fig1.png

[速度方向 = direction of velocity]

(i) Find the expressions for the speed $v_0$ of the ground-state positronium atom and for the energies $E_1$ and $E_2$ of the two photons $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$; and give the values of $v_0$, $E_1$ and $E_2$ when $\theta_1=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ and $\Delta\theta=3.464\times10^{-3}$.

(ii) When the ground-state positronium atom is at rest, find the difference between the energy $E_1$, $E_2$ of each of the two photons $\gamma_1$, $\gamma_2$ and the rest energy of a single free electron.

(3) When a ground-state positronium atom moving relative to the laboratory frame with a speed $v_0$ comparable to the speed of light $c$ annihilates producing two photons, find the energies $E_1$ and $E_2$ of the two produced photons $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$, as well as the relation between the deflection angle $\theta_2$ of the direction of motion of photon $\gamma_2$ relative to the direction of $v_0$ (as shown in the figure) and $\theta_1$; and give the values of $E_1$, $E_2$ and $\theta_2$ when $v_0=\dfrac{c}{2}$ and $\theta_1=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.

Given: the ground-state energy of the hydrogen atom $E^{\mathrm{H}}_{n=1}=-13.60\ \mathrm{eV}$, the electron mass $m_{\mathrm{e}}=0.5110\ \mathrm{MeV}/c^{2}$, and the ratio of the proton mass to the electron mass is $1836$.

Physical constants and formulas that may be used (printed at the beginning of the paper): speed of light in vacuum $c=2.998\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m/s}$; the magnitude of the gravitational acceleration at the Earth's surface is $g$; Planck's constant is $h$, $\hbar=\dfrac{h}{2\pi}$; $\displaystyle\int\frac{1}{1-x^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\ln\frac{1+x}{1-x}+C,\quad |x|<1$.

Problem 1

As shown in the figure, the radii of two plano-convex transparent cylindrical surfaces, an upper one and a lower one, are $R_1$ and $R_2$ respectively, and the two cylindrical surfaces are externally tangent; their sections (planes) are each parallel to their own axes and parallel to each other; the generatrices of the two cylinders passing through the point of tangency are perpendicular to each other. With the help of an optical reading microscope, looking against the Z direction, one can observe the projection onto the X-Y plane of the interference fringes on the upper cylindrical surface near the origin. $R_1$ and $R_2$ are much larger than the maximum gap between the two cylindrical surfaces corresponding to the region of interference of the paraxial rays. The refractive index of air is $n_0=1.00$. Derive the equation of the curve of the projection onto the X-Y plane of the $k$-th order bright fringe.

problems.title: Problem 2

Problem 2

Early one autumn morning, when the air temperature is $4.0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, a water filler comes to the experimental garden to fill a cylindrical stainless-steel distilled-water tank of inner diameter $2.00\ \mathrm{m}$ and height $2.00\ \mathrm{m}$. The tank body conducts heat well. Outside the tank there is a transparent cylindrical observation column of inner diameter $4.00\ \mathrm{cm}$, whose bottom is connected to the tank (the connection is very short) and whose top is open to the atmosphere, as shown in the figure. After filling, the water filler covers the water surface with a layer of light anti-evaporation film (insoluble in water, and without friction against the tank wall), and seals the filling opening at the top of the tank. At this moment the water filler sees from the scale on the observation column that the height of the water in the tank is $1.00\ \mathrm{m}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/cpho-2016-2-2-fig1.png

[观察柱 = observation column; 加水口 = filling opening; 蒸馏水罐 = distilled-water tank]

(1) From early morning to noon the air temperature rises slowly to $24.0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. What is the water level in the observation column at this time? Assume that nobody uses water in the meantime, and that the evaporation of water and the change of the volumes of the tank and the observation column with temperature may be neglected.

(2) From the sealing of the water tank until noon, how much work does the air in the tank do on the surroundings, and how much heat does it absorb? Find the heat capacity of the air in the tank in this process.

Given: the air pressure outside the tank is always the standard atmospheric pressure $p_0=1.01\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{Pa}$; the density of water at $4.0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ is $\rho_0=1.00\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{kg\cdot m^{-3}}$; the average volume expansion coefficient of water over the temperature change is $\kappa=3.03\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}}$; the magnitude of the gravitational acceleration is $g=9.80\ \mathrm{m\cdot s^{-2}}$; absolute zero is $-273.15\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.

Problem 3 [20 points]

Jupiter is the most massive planet in the Solar System (its mass is about 318 times that of the Earth). Assume that the Earth and Jupiter both revolve around the Sun in circular orbits, the two orbits lying in the same plane. Treat the Sun, the Earth and Jupiter as point masses, and neglect the gravitational attraction of the other bodies of the Solar System; moreover, the gravitational attraction between the Earth and Jupiter may be neglected while the Sun is present. The masses of the Sun and of Jupiter are $m_{\mathrm{s}}$ and $m_{\mathrm{j}}$ respectively, and the gravitational constant is $G$. The orbital radii of the Earth and of Jupiter around the Sun are $r_{\mathrm{e}}$ and $r_{\mathrm{j}}$ respectively. Assume that at a certain moment the angle between the line joining the Earth to the Sun and the line joining Jupiter to the Sun is $\theta$. If at this moment the mass of the Sun suddenly became zero, find

(1) the magnitude $v_{\mathrm{ej}}$ of the velocity of the Earth relative to Jupiter at this moment, and the minimum speed $v_0$ needed for the Earth not to be captured by Jupiter's gravity.

(2) Discuss whether the Earth will thereafter revolve around Jupiter; you may use the results of (1) and the data $m_{\mathrm{s}}\approx2.0\times10^{30}\ \mathrm{kg}$, $m_{\mathrm{j}}\approx1.9\times10^{27}\ \mathrm{kg}$, and the orbital period of Jupiter $T_{\mathrm{j}}\approx12\ \mathrm{y}$.

A photomultiplier tube is a device used to convert a light signal into an electrical signal and amplify it. Its structure is shown in Fig. a: it consists mainly of a photocathode, $n$ dynodes and an anode. Between the photocathode and the 1st dynode, between adjacent dynodes, and between the $n$-th dynode and the anode there is in each case a potential difference $V$. The electrons escaping from the photocathode are called photoelectrons; most of them (a fraction $\eta$) are collected on the 1st dynode, and the rest are collected directly on the anode. Each electron collected on the $i$-th dynode ($i=1,\cdots,n$) causes $\delta$ electrons ($\delta>1$) to escape from that electrode; most of the electrons escaping from the $i$-th dynode (a fraction $\sigma$) are collected by the $(i+1)$-th dynode, and the others are collected by the anode; this continues until all the electrons are collected by the anode, so that the signal is amplified. The magnitude of the electron charge is $e$.

Problem 3

A skilled person on a swing can make the swing go higher and higher by standing up and squatting down on the swing seat at the right moments. A person of mass $m$ rides a swing whose seat and suspension rods are both rigid; the masses of the seat and the rods may be neglected, and the mass of the person is assumed to be concentrated at his centre of mass. Each time the person stands fully upright on the swing, the distance from his centre of mass to the suspension point O is $l$; when he squats fully, this distance becomes $l+d$. In reality, standing up and squatting down on the swing are each completed over a certain period of time. As a simple model, assume that at the 1st highest point A the person squats quickly from the fully standing posture to the fully squatting posture, and then swings to the lowest point B, the height difference between A and B being $h_1$; then at B he stands up quickly and fully (with final radial velocity equal to zero), and then swings with the swing to the 2nd highest point C. The trajectory of the person's centre of mass during this process is shown in the figure. After that the person swings back in the same way, repeating the above process, and swings to the 3rd, 4th, etc. highest points. Assume that during standing up and squatting down, the interaction force between the person and the swing is always parallel to the suspension rods. Take the lowest point B as the zero of gravitational potential energy.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/cpho-2017-1-3-fig1.png

(1) Assuming that there is no loss of mechanical energy during the stages in which the person stays fully squatted or stays fully standing, find the mechanical energy of the person's centre of mass in each stage $\rm A\to A'\to B\to B'\to C$, and its changes;

(2) Assume that the losses of mechanical energy $\Delta E$ during the stages in which the person stays fully squatted and stays fully standing are related to the absolute value $\Delta h$ of the height difference between the beginning and the end of the stage by, respectively,

$$\Delta E=k_1mg(h_0+\Delta h),\quad 0<k_1<1,\ \text{staying fully squatted};$$
$$\Delta E=k_2mg(h_0'+\Delta h),\quad 0<k_2<1,\ \text{staying fully standing}.$$

Here $k_1$, $k_2$, $h_0$ and $h_0'$ are constants and $g$ is the magnitude of the gravitational acceleration. Find

(i) the relation between the height $h_n$ of the $n$-th highest point and the height $h_{n+1}$ of the $(n+1)$-th highest point, both relative to the point B;

(ii) the relation between $h_n$ and $h_1$, and the relation between $h_{n+1}-h_n$ and $h_1$.

Problem 7

(1) Einstein's equivalence principle can be stated as follows: the laws of physics in the presence of gravitation are the same as the laws of physics in a reference frame with a suitable acceleration but without gravitation. As an example, consider the following two situations:

(i) When a beam of light propagates from a place of lower gravitational potential to a place of higher gravitational potential, its wavelength becomes longer; this phenomenon is called gravitational redshift. Suppose that at a point A near the surface of a spherical star with uniform mass distribution, light of wavelength $\lambda_0$ is emitted vertically upward, and a fixed receiver is placed at a point B located at height $L$ vertically above A. Find the wavelength $\lambda'$ of the light received by the receiver at B. The mass of the star is $M$ and its radius is $R$ ($R\gg L$); the gravitational field satisfies the weak-field condition, so Newtonian gravitational theory may be applied; the speed of light in vacuum is $c$ and the gravitational constant is $G$.

(ii) As shown in the figure, suppose that in the absence of gravitation there is a box of length $L$, with a laser receiver and a laser emitter placed at B and A on the upper and lower faces of the box respectively. At time $t=0$ the box starts from zero initial velocity and moves with uniform acceleration of magnitude $a$ along the direction AB ($aL\ll c^2$); at the same time a laser beam of wavelength $\lambda_0$ is emitted from A. According to special relativity, find the wavelength $\lambda''$ of the laser light received by the receiver at B.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/cpho-2017-1-7-fig1.png

(iii) According to the equivalence principle, compare the results of (i) and (ii): for the laws of physics to be the same in situations (i) and (ii), how large should $a$ in (ii) be?

(2) The first experimental verification of the gravitational redshift was carried out near the surface of the Earth using a Mössbauer detector; a Mössbauer detector can resolve the energy of gamma photons with extremely high precision. Following part (1)(i), near the surface of the Earth a stationary gamma radiation source is placed at A, the frequency of the emitted gamma photons being $\nu_0$; a Mössbauer detector is placed at B, and suppose that in its own rest frame this detector can only detect gamma photons of frequency $\nu_0$. In order to detect the gamma photons emitted from A, the Mössbauer detector needs a certain vertically downward velocity. In solid materials, after interactions are taken into account, the concept of "quasiparticles" can be used to study the physical properties of the material. The relation between the kinetic energy and the momentum of a quasiparticle may differ from that of a real particle. When an external electric or magnetic field is applied, the motion of a quasiparticle can often be treated by the methods of classical mechanics. In a certain two-dimensional interface structure there are quasiparticles with charge $q$ and effective mass $m$, which can move only in the $x$-$y$ plane; the relation between their kinetic energy $K$ and the magnitude $p$ of their momentum can be expressed as $K=\frac{p^2}{2m}+\alpha p$, where $\alpha$ is a positive constant.

(1) For a real free particle of mass $m$, the relation between the kinetic energy $K$ and the magnitude $p$ of the momentum can be expressed as $K=\frac{p^2}{2m}$. Starting from the work-energy theorem, derive the relation between the velocity $\boldsymbol{v}$ of the particle's motion and its momentum $\boldsymbol{p}$.

(2) Following the method of (1), derive the relation between the velocity $\boldsymbol{v}$ of the quasiparticle's motion and its momentum $\boldsymbol{p}$.

(3) Express the magnitude of the quasiparticle's velocity in terms of its kinetic energy.

(4) The two-dimensional interface structure is placed in a uniform magnetic field directed along the positive $z$ axis, with magnetic induction of magnitude $B$. Find the radius, the period and the magnitude of the angular momentum of the uniform circular motion of a quasiparticle with kinetic energy $K$.

If the electric field is along the positive $x$ axis with field strength of magnitude $E$, find the components $a_x$ and $a_y$ of the acceleration of the quasiparticle's motion when its speed is $v$ ($v\neq\alpha$) and its direction makes an angle $\theta$ with the positive $x$ axis.

Problem 8

Thermal radiation is incident on a mirror; the mirror can use the radiation pressure of the thermal radiation to do work on the surroundings. This process can be studied from the point of view of dynamics or of thermodynamics. For simplicity, the thermal radiation is regarded as one-dimensional black-body radiation incident normally on a plane ideal reflecting (totally reflecting) mirror. The radiation pressure on the mirror is balanced by an external resistive force, so that the mirror moves uniformly with velocity $v$, in the same direction as the incident radiation. It is known that, in the laboratory frame, the spectrum of one-dimensional black-body radiation at temperature $T$ (the radiant energy emitted per unit time per unit frequency interval near frequency $\nu$) is $\varphi(\nu,T)=\frac{2h\nu}{\mathrm{e}^{h\nu/kT}-1}$, where $h$ is the Planck constant and $k$ is the Boltzmann constant. The speed of light in vacuum is $c$.

(1) Starting from the dynamical viewpoint of collisions between the photons of the one-dimensional black-body radiation and the moving ideal mirror, calculate, in the laboratory frame, the efficiency $\eta$ with which the mirror uses the photon energy to do work against the resistive force.

(2) From the thermodynamic point of view, the incidence of the radiation and the subsequent reflection can be regarded as a tiny ideal heat-engine cycle undergone by the mirror as the working substance: the incidence process can be regarded as the mirror absorbing heat from a high-temperature heat reservoir, the reflection process as the mirror releasing heat to a low-temperature heat reservoir, and finally the mirror returns to its original state. On the basis of this viewpoint, prove that in the rest frame of the mirror both the incident radiation and the reflected radiation are one-dimensional black-body radiation, and calculate the efficiency of this heat engine in the rest frame of the mirror.

(3) Calculate the efficiency of this heat engine in the laboratory frame.

(1) Neglecting the level width of the excited state, find the recoil energy, and the difference between the frequencies of the photon emitted when $^{57}\mathrm{Fe}$ makes the transition from the first excited state to the ground state in the cases where nuclear recoil is taken into account and where it is not.

Problem 3

Long-term, high-precision observation of the small variations of the gravitational acceleration at the Earth's surface and of their distribution with superconducting gravimeters can provide information on the internal structure of the Earth, such as mantle motion, mass distribution, solid-Earth tides, groundwater and mineral distribution, as well as external data such as ocean tides and climate change. Superconducting gravimeters have high sensitivity (up to $10^{-9}$ of the gravitational acceleration at the Earth's surface) and strong stability, and are the gravity-observation instruments widely used in the Earth sciences today. With the increase in the number of superconducting gravimeters distributed around the world, the establishment of observation networks and data sharing, new opportunities are offered for the development of the Earth sciences, the precise testing of the law of universal gravitation, and so on. 1) Assume that the Earth can be regarded as a uniform sphere of radius 6370 km, with gravitational acceleration at its surface $g_0=9.80\ \mathrm{m\cdot s^{-2}}$ (neglect the rotation of the Earth). Problem 4

A car obtains its power from the combustion of the air and petrol in the engine cylinders; the output power of the engine is proportional to the mass of air entering the cylinders. To increase the power, many cars are fitted with a turbocharger, which compresses the air before it enters the engine cylinders so as to increase the air density; to increase the air density further, an intercooler is also used, so that the air enters the cylinders after its temperature has been lowered. In a typical arrangement, the initial pressure of the air entering the turbocharger is one atmosphere, $p_0=1.01\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{Pa}$, and its temperature is $T_0=15^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$; after passing through the turbocharger the air is adiabatically compressed to $p_1=1.45\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{Pa}$; then, passing through the intercooler, the air is cooled at constant pressure to the initial temperature $T_0$ and fills the cylinder. Assume that air is an ideal gas; the cylinder volume is known to be $V_0=400\ \mathrm{cm^3}$, the molar mass of air $M=29.0\ \mathrm{g\cdot mol^{-1}}$, the ratio of molar heat capacities $\gamma=7/5$, and the universal gas constant $R=8.31\ \mathrm{J\cdot K^{-1}\cdot mol^{-1}}$.

1) Find the mass of the air in the cylinder in this case; compared with the case without turbocharging and cooling, by what factor is the output power of the engine increased?

2) If there is no intercooler and the air, after being compressed by the turbocharger only, is fed into the cylinder, what is the corresponding mass of air? Compared with the case without turbocharging, by what factor is the output power of the engine increased?

3) In the thermodynamic processes through the turbocharger and the intercooler, find the work done by the surroundings on the gas entering the cylinder, and the entropy change of the gas in the cylinder in each of the two processes above.

Problem 6

Looking up at the starry sky can stimulate people's boundless imagination. With the progress of science and technology, people's understanding of the universe keeps deepening; the solution of the mystery of the missing neutrinos, the direct detection of gravitational waves and the recent photograph of a black hole have aroused wide public interest in exploring the universe. How did humankind, using limited equipment, observe and study the vast universe and its important constituents, the stars? Can members of the public with a basic knowledge of high-school physics understand quantitatively the internal and external properties of a star, such as its size, mass, age, lifetime, composition and energy-production mechanism? Taking as an example the star on which we depend for our existence, the Sun, and following the historical development, try to build a model of the Sun step by step from the simple to the complex. Since the interior of the Sun cannot be observed directly, the model built must be tested from many aspects, such as age, radius, surface temperature, energy output, neutrino flux, and so on, all of which must be mutually self-consistent within the same model.

The following are known: the radius of the Earth is 6370 km; the gravitational constant $G=6.67\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{N\cdot m^2\cdot kg^{-2}}$; the Stefan–Boltzmann constant $\sigma=5.67\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{W\cdot m^{-2}\cdot K^{-4}}$; the Boltzmann constant $k_{\mathrm{B}}=1.38\times10^{-23}\ \mathrm{J\cdot K^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e=1.602\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$; the electron mass $m_{\mathrm{e}}=0.51\ \mathrm{MeV}/c^2$; the proton mass $m_{\mathrm{p}}=938.3\ \mathrm{MeV}/c^2$; the deuteron mass $m_{\mathrm{D}}=1875.6\ \mathrm{MeV}/c^2$; the $^{3}\mathrm{He}$ nucleus mass $m_{^3\mathrm{He}}=2808.4\ \mathrm{MeV}/c^2$; the $^{4}\mathrm{He}$ nucleus mass $m_{^4\mathrm{He}}=3727.5\ \mathrm{MeV}/c$; the speed of light in vacuum $c=3.00\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\cdot s^{-1}}$.

1) The Zhoubi Suanjing ("The Arithmetical Classic of the Gnomon", originally titled Zhoubi), a book written more than two thousand years ago, describes a method for measuring the ratio of the diameter $D$ of the Sun to the Sun–Earth distance $S_{\mathrm{SE}}$ (also called 1 astronomical unit): take a long bamboo pole and chisel out its nodes so that its inside is open throughout; the inner diameter of the bamboo pole is $d$. Point this bamboo pole at the Sun and change the length $L$ of the pole until the solar disc exactly fills the inner tube of the bamboo pole.

i) Give the relation between the angular diameter of the Sun ($\Phi=D/S_{\mathrm{SE}}$) and $d$ and $L$;

ii) to reduce the error, $L$ must be long enough; what other methods are there to reduce the error?

iii) It is measured that $d=1$ cun and $L=8$ chi (10 cun make one chi); estimate the value of $\Phi$.

2) At certain special times (for example on 6 June 2012) the Earth, Venus and the Sun lie almost on one straight line; observed from the Earth, Venus then looks like a small black dot set in the solar disc and moves slowly; this is called a transit of Venus, as shown in Fig. a. The British astronomer Halley proposed in 1716 that observations of the transit of Venus be made jointly all over the world in order to measure the angular diameter of the Sun and the Sun–Earth distance. The periods of revolution of the Earth and of Venus, which revolve around the Sun in the same sense, are known to be 365.256 days and 224.701 days respectively, and the inclination between their orbital planes is very small. Neglect the rotation of the Earth.

Fig. a. Schematic diagram of the transit of Venus on 6 June 2012 [凌始外切 = first contact (start of transit, external tangency); 凌始内切 = second contact (start of transit, internal tangency); 凌甚 = greatest transit; 凌终内切 = third contact (end of transit, internal tangency); 凌终外切 = fourth contact (end of transit, external tangency)]

i) The orbits of the Earth and of Venus can both be regarded as circles; find the ratio $r_{\mathrm{VE}}$ of the Sun–Venus distance $S_{\mathrm{SV}}$ to the Sun–Earth distance $S_{\mathrm{SE}}$;

ii) on 6 June 2012, the transit of Venus was observed at a certain place as shown in Fig. a; calculate the ratio of the chord length $D_{\mathrm{P}}$ swept across the solar disc during the transit of Venus to the Sun–Earth distance $S_{\mathrm{SE}}$. If the distance between this chord and the centre of the disc is $h_{\mathrm{P}}=5D/16$, what is the angular diameter $\Phi$ of the Sun?

iii) To measure the Sun–Earth distance, the transit of Venus must be observed from different places on the Earth's surface, as shown in Fig. b. Suppose that two observers P and P′ on the same meridian, whose straight-line distance (projected onto the direction perpendicular to the direction of observation) is $H$, observe the transit of Venus at the same time. For P, the path of Venus on the solar disc is AB and the observed transit time (the time interval during which the centre of Venus sweeps across the solar disc) is $t_{\mathrm{P}}$; for P′, the path of Venus on the solar disc is A′B′ and the observed transit time is $t_{\mathrm{P'}}$. Find the expression for the Sun–Earth distance $S_{\mathrm{SE}}$ (in terms of $\Phi$, $r_{\mathrm{VE}}$, $T_{\mathrm{E}}$, $T_{\mathrm{V}}$, $t_{\mathrm{P}}$, $t_{\mathrm{P'}}$, $H$, etc.).

Fig. b. Schematic diagram of the transit of Venus [地球 = Earth; 金星 = Venus; 太阳 = Sun]

iv) The latitudes of Beijing and Hong Kong are known to be $39.5^{\circ}$ and $22.5^{\circ}$ respectively; on 6 June 2012 the transit times of Venus observed in Beijing and in Hong Kong were respectively $t_{\mathrm{P}}=6:21:57$ and $t_{\mathrm{P'}}=6:19:31$. The irradiance of solar radiation received by the Earth on a surface perpendicular to the direction of the solar radiation is $I=1.37\ \mathrm{kW\cdot m^{-2}}$. Find

i) the total energy received by the Earth from the Sun per unit time;

ii) the ratio of the energy consumed by the world population of 7 billion to the solar energy received by the Earth (assume that the annual energy consumption per person is 3 tonnes of standard coal, and that 1 kg of standard coal can generate 4 kWh of electricity);

iii) the total energy radiated by the Sun per unit time;

iv) estimate the surface temperature of the Sun.

4) i) Calculate the total mass and the mean density of the Sun;

ii) if the energy of the Sun came from chemical reactions, with the energy released per unit mass equal to that of coal, how long could it last, calculated with the energy the Sun now radiates per unit time? The Sun has existed as a star for about 5 billion years or more; by what factor, then, should its efficiency of energy production exceed that of chemical reactions?

5) Spectral analysis shows that the main constituent of the Sun is hydrogen; the basic nuclear fusion reactions involving hydrogen are as follows:

$$\mathrm{P}+\mathrm{P}\to\mathrm{D}+\mathrm{e}^{+}+\nu_{\mathrm{e}}\qquad\text{(a)}$$

$$\mathrm{D}+\mathrm{P}\to{}^{3}\mathrm{He}+\gamma\qquad\text{(b)}$$

$${}^{3}\mathrm{He}+{}^{3}\mathrm{He}\to{}^{4}\mathrm{He}+\mathrm{P}+\mathrm{P}\qquad\text{(c)}$$

The positrons produced in the above nuclear fusion processes will annihilate, and the neutrinos will escape. Atomic nuclei are all positively charged and repel one another; only when the temperature is very high can their kinetic energy overcome the Coulomb repulsion, so that fusion reactions take place. When the temperature is high enough, all atoms are ionized into atomic nuclei and electrons and are in a plasma state. (Here neglect the energy carried away by the neutrinos, and also the unfused hydrogen carried away by the solar wind.)

i) To maintain the radiation of the Sun, how many protons (hydrogen nuclei) must be consumed per unit time?

ii) At present 71% of the mass of the Sun is hydrogen; at this rate of consumption, for at most how many more years can it be maintained? Also calculate the proton–proton reaction probability per unit time (the ratio of the number of particles reacting per unit time to the total number of particles) $P_{\mathrm{PP}}$;

iii) the number of escaping neutrinos does not decrease during propagation; how many neutrinos reach the Earth per unit time per unit area perpendicular to the direction of the solar radiation? (The number of electron neutrinos actually reaching the Earth is only 35% of the theoretical value, but when the numbers of the other two kinds of neutrinos are added, it agrees with the theoretical value; this shows that some electron neutrinos are converted into other kinds of neutrinos during propagation, which is related to neutrino oscillations; the related achievements were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2002 and 2015.)

iv) How much mass does the Sun lose per unit time because of its radiation?

6) The probability $P$ of a fusion reaction depends on the temperature $T$ of the plasma, and the higher the particle number density $n$ (the number of particles per unit volume), the higher the reaction probability; the relation is $P=nR(T)$, where $R(T)$ is called the reaction rate. Fig. c gives the relation between the reaction rates of three kinds of fusion and the temperature; estimate the lower limit of the temperature of the solar core region (whose radius is about one quarter of the solar radius) in which nuclear fusion reactions can take place.

Fig. c. Curves of the reaction rate versus temperature

7) Estimate the maximum energy carried away by a single neutrino, and estimate the maximum relative error of the calculation of the radiated energy in part 5) caused by neglecting the energy carried away by the neutrinos.

8) From the above calculations, the mass of the Sun decreases gradually; then the period and the mean orbital radius of the Earth's revolution around the Sun will also change. Calculate

i) the mass decrease $\Delta M$ due to radiation within one hundred million years;

ii) the resulting change of the period of the Earth's revolution.

The decorative design of its conference hall showed both the energy-saving and environmental concepts of Chinese architecture and the characteristics of Zhejiang's bamboo culture. Figure a shows an enlarged photograph of part of the micro-perforated bamboo-panel decoration used on part of the walls; this decoration also achieves resonant absorption of sound waves. The bamboo panels have a series of rectangular micro-holes of different areas arranged periodically; after a sound wave enters a micro-hole, it makes the air column in the micro-hole perform simple harmonic vibrations. A single micro-hole together with the air layer behind the bamboo panel can be simplified as a Helmholtz resonator, as shown in Figure b. Assume that all micro-holes have depth $l$, that the volume of the air cavity behind a single micro-hole is $V_0$, and that the cross-sectional area of a micro-hole is $S$. $$v_{\rm s} = \sqrt{\frac{\kappa}{\rho}}$$

where $\kappa$ is the ratio of the increase $\Delta p$ in the gas pressure to the relative change of its volume $V$:

It is known that under standard conditions ($273\ {\rm K}$, $1\ {\rm atm} = 1.01\times10^{5}\ {\rm Pa}$) the molar mass of air (which may be regarded as an ideal gas) is $M_{\rm mol} = 29.0\ {\rm g/mol}$, the heat capacity ratio is $\gamma = \dfrac{7}{5}$, and the universal gas constant is $R = 8.31\ {\rm J/(K\cdot mol)}$.

problems.title: Problem 6
problems.problem:
Problem 6

In cosmic rays there are large numbers of $\pi$ mesons flying at high speeds; they decay into a $\mu$ lepton and a $\mu$-type antineutrino $\bar{\nu}_\mu$:

$$\pi \to \mu + \bar{\nu}_\mu$$

The rest masses of the $\pi$ meson and of the $\mu$ lepton are known to be $m_\pi = 139.57061\ {\rm MeV}/c^2$ and $m_\mu = 105.65837\ {\rm MeV}/c^2$ respectively, and the rest mass of the antineutrino $\bar{\nu}_\mu$ is approximately zero. In the laboratory frame the speed of flight of the $\pi$ meson is measured to be $\boldsymbol{v} = 0.965\boldsymbol{c}$ ($c = 3.00\times10^{8}\ {\rm m/s}$ is the speed of light in vacuum).

1) Find the maximum and minimum speeds of the $\mu$ lepton produced in the above decay;

2) A $\mu$ lepton produced in the above decay flies vertically downward from a height of $10000\ {\rm m}$ above the ground. The half-life of the $\mu$ lepton at rest is known to be $T_{\frac{1}{2}}^{(0)} = 1.523\ \mu{\rm s}$. Find the maximum probability that an observer on the ground can observe the $\mu$ lepton.

problems.title: Problem 7
problems.problem:
Problem 7

Lightning is one of the most spectacular natural phenomena on Earth. People have studied lightning extensively, and in recent years new phenomena have also been observed, such as transient luminous events and gamma-ray bursts caused by lightning. Lightning is usually produced by the discharge of thunderclouds (6–12 km above the ground); most lightning occurs inside the clouds and a small part reaches the ground. Because the ice-crystal particles inside the cloud collide with one another, the small ice-crystal particles become positively charged and float up with the air flow to the top of the cloud, while the larger particles become negatively charged and fall to the bottom of the cloud (see Figure a). Intra-cloud lightning neutralizes the positive and negative charges inside the cloud, whereas cloud-to-ground lightning releases the negative charge to the ground.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/cpho-2019-2-7-fig1.png

Figure a. Schematic diagram of the charge distribution of a thundercloud

[Labels in the figure: 闪电 = lightning; 地面 = ground.]

1) The electric field inside a thundercloud in a certain cylindrical region high in the air is measured with an electric-field meter carried by a high-altitude balloon; its strength may be regarded as uniformly distributed, with magnitude $0.15\ {\rm MV/m}$. The central axis of this cylindrical region is perpendicular to the ground, its radius is $2.5\ {\rm km}$ and its height is $1.0\ {\rm km}$. Find the potential difference between the upper and lower ends of this region, the total amount of positive charge, and the total electric energy carried. The permittivity of vacuum is known to be $\varepsilon_0 = 8.85\times10^{-12}\ {\rm F/m}$.

2) During the electrification process, the charges at the upper and lower ends of a thundercloud increase exponentially with time. When the electric field at the Earth's surface exceeds $1.0\ {\rm kV/m}$, cloud-to-ground lightning occurs, so the surface electric field rarely exceeds $10\ {\rm kV/m}$. Suppose that the thundercloud described in 1) slowly moves downward as a whole from high in the air until its negative-charge layer is at a height of $6.0\ {\rm km}$ above the ground, where it temporarily remains stable. The ground is a good conductor. Estimate the strength of the surface electric field produced by this thundercloud directly below it.

3) Cloud-to-ground lightning is usually triggered by point discharge from the negatively charged ice-crystal particles at the bottom of a charged thundercloud: first a thin discharge path pointing toward the ground forms (with a diameter of the order of centimetres); this thin path extends downward with time and causes the surrounding air to be ionized continuously, gradually forming a thick cylindrical charged body with the original thin path as its axis (with cross-section of constant size), and finally a cloud-to-ground lightning channel forms near the ground. This lightning channel is perpendicular to the ground, the total amount of negative charge is $2.5\ {\rm C}$ (the charge in the original thin discharge path is relatively very small), and the electric field strength inside the lightning channel (excluding the central thin discharge path) is everywhere of the same magnitude. Assume that the length of the lightning channel is much greater than its diameter, that the diameter of the lightning channel is much greater than the diameter of the central thin discharge path, and that during the extremely short time before the lightning channel connects the cloud to the ground, the charge distribution inside the lightning channel may be regarded as steady. The breakdown threshold of the atmospheric electric field is known to be $3.0\ {\rm MV/m}$. Estimate the diameter of this cloud-to-ground lightning channel, and derive the expression for the radial distribution of the charge density inside the lightning channel (excluding the central thin discharge path).

4) After the lightning channel connects the cloud and the ground, the negative charges at the bottom of the cloud and inside the channel rapidly flow to the ground; the temperature of the lightning region suddenly rises to tens of thousands of degrees Celsius, so that the air in it is ionized and forms a plasma, emitting strong light, while the channel expands violently, producing thunder. The discharge current of the lightning can reach several tens of thousands of amperes within about $10\ \mu{\rm s}$. At the bottom of the channel (near the ground) strong radio waves with frequencies of about $30\ {\rm kHz}$ are radiated in all directions. Since electromagnetic waves with frequencies below $20\ {\rm MHz}$ (the so-called ionospheric cut-off frequency) cannot enter the interior of the ionosphere, these radio waves heat the plasma at the bottom of the ionosphere (about $80\ {\rm km}$ above the ground); once the lightning current exceeds a certain threshold, this causes the bottom of the ionosphere to glow instantaneously, forming a ring of light centred at the bottom of the ionosphere directly above the source of the strong radio waves (the bottom of the channel), whose maximum diameter can extend to several hundred kilometres. Sketch a diagram of the physical process of the formation and expansion of the ring of light at the bottom of the ionosphere, and calculate the radial speed of expansion of the ring of light when its radius is $100\ {\rm km}$.

5) The microwave-bubble model of ball lightning holds that ball lightning is a spherical plasma microwave cavity (bubble). When the lightning microwaves are rather weak and insufficient to form a microwave bubble, they radiate toward outer space and pass through the ionosphere, and can be observed by satellites. In fact, satellites have indeed observed this kind of microwave radiation. However, the signals observed by satellites are easily disturbed by ionospheric dispersion, whereas a high-altitude balloon carrying a detector can reach above the thundercloud for observation, so as to avoid such disturbances. In order to observe, at a height of $12\ {\rm km}$ above the ground, the microwave signals emitted by lightning, a high-altitude helium balloon with a payload (including the balloon material and the detector) of $50\ {\rm kg}$ is to be kept floating in this region. Find the volume of this balloon when it floats in that high-altitude region. It is known that below a height of $12\ {\rm km}$ above the ground the atmospheric temperature decreases by $5.0\ {\rm K}$ for every $1\ {\rm km}$ rise in height; the ground temperature is $T_0 = 290\ {\rm K}$, the ground pressure is $p_0 = 1.01\times10^{5}\ {\rm pa}$, the molar mass of air is $M = 29\ {\rm g/mol}$; the density of helium in the balloon (its value at a height of $12\ {\rm km}$ above the ground) is $\rho_{\rm He} = 0.18\ {\rm kg/m^3}$; the gravitational acceleration is $g = 9.8\ {\rm m/s^2}$, and the universal gas constant is $R = 8.31\ {\rm J/(K\cdot mol)}$.

Problem 1

China's large scientific facility, the Spallation Neutron Source, was completed and put into operation in 2018; it has wide applications in many fields. Historically, Chadwick first confirmed the existence of the neutron in 1932 and measured its mass; in 1939 Hahn and co-workers discovered that bombarding uranium nuclei with neutrons can make them split, at the same time releasing neutrons and triggering a chain reaction. In order for the chain reaction to proceed in a sustained and controllable way, the neutrons released by the uranium nuclei can be slowed down (moderated) by elastic collisions. Relativistic effects are not to be considered.

(1) Chadwick bombarded stationary target nuclei of mass $m_1$ (hydrogen nuclei H or nitrogen nuclei $^{14}\mathrm{N}$, of mass $m_{\mathrm{H}}$ or $14m_{\mathrm{H}}$) with neutrons (of mass $m$) and observed their motion. Let the angle between the outgoing momentum of the target nucleus and the initial momentum of the incident neutron be $\alpha$. Derive the relations of the outgoing speed $v_1$ of the target nucleus and of the final speed $v$ of the neutron, respectively, to the initial speed $v_0$ of the neutron. In this experiment the maximum outgoing speed of the hydrogen nuclei was measured to be $3.30\times10^{7}\,\mathrm{m/s}$, and the maximum outgoing speed of the nitrogen nuclei $4.70\times10^{6}\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Find the values of $m$ and $v_0$.

(2) In the above experiment a nitrogen nucleus may also be struck successively by a beam of neutrons. Suppose the nitrogen nucleus is initially at rest, every neutron colliding with it has speed $v_0$, and every collision gives the largest possible increase of the speed of the nitrogen nucleus. Calculate after how many collisions the kinetic energy of the nitrogen nucleus is approximately equal to the initial kinetic energy of a neutron.

(3) Suppose the neutrons slowed down by many collisions are in thermal equilibrium, their speeds obeying the Maxwell distribution

$$f(v)=4\pi\left(\frac{m}{2\pi k_{\mathrm{B}}T}\right)^{3/2}v^{2}\,\mathrm{e}^{-\frac{mv^{2}}{2k_{\mathrm{B}}T}},$$

where $k_{\mathrm{B}}$ is the Boltzmann constant and $T$ is the absolute temperature of the system. Calculate, at thermal equilibrium, the kinetic energy corresponding to the most probable speed of the neutrons, and the most probable kinetic energy.

problems.title: Problem 2

Problem 2

When two conducting spheres in an electric field come close to each other, the electric field between the conducting spheres is markedly enhanced. This problem explores this phenomenon. The vacuum permittivity $\varepsilon_0$ is known.

(1) The centre of an isolated conducting sphere of radius $R_0$ is at distance $a$ ($a>R_0$) from a stationary point charge $Q$. Find the magnitude of the image charge and its position.

(2) The conducting sphere is placed in a uniform external electric field of magnitude $E_0$; this external field can be regarded as produced, at the midpoint of the line joining them, by two equal and opposite point charges $\pm Q$ very far apart. Prove that the action of the induced charge of the conducting sphere is equivalent to an electric dipole formed by two image charges, and find the relation between the dipole moment of this electric dipole and the external field $E_0$.

(3) Outside the conducting sphere, two equal and opposite point charges $\pm q$ are separated by $\Delta l$; the electric dipole $q\Delta\boldsymbol{l}$ they form is placed radially near the conducting sphere of radius $R_0$, with the centre of the dipole at distance $r$ ($r\gg\Delta l$) from the centre of the conducting sphere. Find the magnitude of the image dipole moment of this dipole in the conducting sphere.

(4) In a uniform external electric field of magnitude $E_0$, two conducting spheres of radius $R_0$ are placed along the direction of the external field, their centres a distance $r$ ($r>2R_0$) apart. Find the distribution of the electric potential at any point $\mathrm{P}'(x,y)$ outside the conducting spheres in the plane through the two centres, and the distribution of the field strength along the direction of the line joining the two centres (recurrence relations may be used). Take the midpoint of the line joining the two centres as the origin of coordinates and the direction of this line as the $X$ axis.

(5) Prove that, if breakdown discharge is not considered, when the above two conductors are slowly brought infinitely close to each other, the electric field at the midpoint of the line joining the centres of the two spheres tends to infinity because of electrostatic induction.

Problem 3

A quantum heat engine is a heat engine that runs a cycle with quantum matter as the working substance. Below, a two-level atomic system is taken as an example to describe the working principle of a quantum heat engine. The average energy of a two-level atom is defined as

$$\langle E\rangle=p_0\cdot E_0+p_1\cdot E_1,$$

where $E_0$, $p_0$ and $E_1$, $p_1$ denote the energies and probabilities of the atom being in the ground state and in the excited state, respectively. For simplicity, assume $E_0=0$; during the cycle the energy difference between the excited state and the ground state is an adjustable parameter. The probability that the atom is in a state of energy $E$ obeys the Boltzmann distribution

$$p\propto\mathrm{e}^{-E/(k_{\mathrm{B}}T)},$$

where $T$ is the thermodynamic temperature and $k_{\mathrm{B}}$ is the Boltzmann constant. In a quasi-static process the change of the average energy is

$$\mathrm{d}\langle E\rangle=p_1\,\mathrm{d}E_1+E_1\,\mathrm{d}p_1,$$

where $p_1\,\mathrm{d}E_1$ is the energy change caused by the change of the energy level, corresponding to the work $\text{đ}W$ done by the surroundings on the two-level atomic system, and $E_1\,\mathrm{d}p_1$ is the energy change caused by the change of the probability, corresponding to the heat $\text{đ}Q$ transferred by the surroundings to the two-level atomic system.

(1) The two-level atomic system is put in contact with a heat reservoir of temperature $T$. Find the probability $p_0$ that the two-level atomic system is in the ground state and the probability $p_1$ that it is in the excited state at thermal equilibrium.

(2) The $P$-$V$ diagram of the classical Otto cycle is shown in Figure 2a, where A→B and C→D are isochoric processes and B→C and D→A are adiabatic processes. Sketch the relation between the energy difference $E_1$ of the two levels and the excited-state probability $p_1$ during the quantum Otto cycle, and calculate the heat transferred, the increase of internal energy and the work done on the surroundings in each of the four processes of the quantum Otto cycle.

Figure 2a [绝热 = adiabatic]

Assuming that the temperature $T_h$ of the hot reservoir and the temperature $T_l$ of the cold reservoir in the quantum Carnot cycle are equal, respectively, to the highest and the lowest temperature of the quantum Otto cycle, compare the efficiencies of the quantum Otto engine and the quantum Carnot engine.

Problem 5

Interstellar medium exists in the vast cosmic space between the stars. Under the action of cosmic rays, molecules of the interstellar medium lose some of their electrons and become positive ions, while the electrons wander free, forming a plasma state. A pulsar is a rapidly rotating neutron star with an extremely strong magnetic field; the electromagnetic radiation from it observed on the Earth is a pulsed signal. Pulsar signals can be used for interstellar navigation and high-precision timekeeping; for this it is necessary to obtain the precise times of arrival of the pulses at the Earth, and to study the phase changes and dispersion of their electromagnetic radiation.

The distance from a pulsar to the Earth is $d$, and the mean number density of electrons in the interstellar medium is $n_{\mathrm{e}}$ (of the order of $10^{4}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}$). Assume that there is a uniform static magnetic field $B$ in the medium (of the order of $10^{-10}\,\mathrm{T}$), directed parallel to the propagation direction of the electromagnetic waves. The electron mass $m_{\mathrm{e}}$, the electron charge $-e$ ($e>0$), the vacuum permittivity $\varepsilon_0$ and the speed of light in vacuum $c$ are known.

(1) Take the direction of the electromagnetic radiation from the pulsar to the Earth as the positive $z$ direction. For an electromagnetic wave of frequency $f$ the electric field is $E_x=E_0\cos(kz-2\pi ft)$, $E_y=E_0\cos\left(kz-2\pi ft\pm\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$, where $E_0$ and $k$ are the amplitude and the wave number of the electromagnetic wave, respectively. For simplicity, take $E_0$ to be constant and neglect the action of the magnetic field of the electromagnetic wave itself on the electrons. Find the gyration radius $R_{\mathrm{e}}$ of the electron motion.

(2) When a pulsar signal propagates in the interstellar medium, dispersion occurs; its propagation speed (the magnitude $v_{\mathrm{g}}$ of the group velocity) depends on the rate of change of the frequency of the electromagnetic wave with respect to the wave number: $v_{\mathrm{g}}=2\pi\dfrac{\mathrm{d}f}{\mathrm{d}k}$. Find the lowest frequency $f_{\mathrm{c}}$ of the electromagnetic waves of the pulsar signal that can pass through the medium and reach the Earth.

(3) Assuming that the mean electron number density $n_{\mathrm{e}}$ of the interstellar medium stays constant along the propagation path of the pulsar signal, by how much is the time of arrival at the Earth of the electromagnetic wave of frequency $f$ in the pulsar signal delayed compared with its propagation time in vacuum?

(4) It is observed that the electromagnetic waves of frequency $f$ that leave the pulsar simultaneously show a phase difference on arrival at the Earth. Find this phase difference (the approximations $\dfrac{e}{2\pi}\sqrt{\dfrac{n_{\mathrm{e}}}{\varepsilon_0m_{\mathrm{e}}}}\ll f$, $\dfrac{eB}{2\pi m_{\mathrm{e}}}\ll f$ may be used).

(5) If over an interval of length $a$ along the propagation path the electron number density shows a fluctuation $\Delta n_{\mathrm{e}}$, find the phase shift, caused by the fluctuation of the electron number density, of the electromagnetic wave of frequency $f$ in the pulsar signal after it passes through this interval.

Problem 6

Antiparticles were first predicted by Dirac's theory. In 1932, while studying cosmic rays, Anderson discovered the antiparticle of the electron, the positron. Since then, further antiparticles such as the antiproton have been discovered one after another.

Antiprotons can be produced by bombarding a stationary proton target with a beam of high-energy protons of energy $6.8\,\mathrm{GeV}$ per particle; the reaction is

$$\mathrm{p}+\mathrm{p}\to\mathrm{p}+\mathrm{p}+\underbrace{\mathrm{p}+\bar{\mathrm{p}}}_{\hookrightarrow\ \pi^{-}+\cdots}$$

When protons and antiprotons annihilate, $\pi^{-}$ mesons can be produced, so the antiproton beam is also accompanied by a large number of $\pi^{-}$ mesons. Figure 6a is a schematic diagram of the experimental set-up for detecting antiprotons. The stream of antiprotons $\bar{\mathrm{p}}$ and $\pi^{-}$ mesons passes successively through the scintillation counters $\mathrm{S}_1$, $\mathrm{S}_2$ and $\mathrm{S}_3$; $\mathrm{S}_1$ and $\mathrm{S}_2$ are a distance $l=12\,\mathrm{m}$ apart, and the Cherenkov counters $\mathrm{C}_1$ and $\mathrm{C}_2$ are placed between $\mathrm{S}_2$ and $\mathrm{S}_3$. A Cherenkov counter determines the speed of a charged particle by detecting Cherenkov radiation (the electromagnetic radiation excited when a charged particle moves in a medium faster than the speed of light in the medium). $\mathrm{C}_1$ records only the faster $\pi^{-}$ mesons, and $\mathrm{C}_2$ records only the slower antiprotons. In the experiment, the role of $\mathrm{S}_3$ is to check whether the preceding counting results are genuine.

(1) In the above reaction, assuming that the protons and the antiproton in the final state have approximately equal velocities, find the time $t_{\bar{\mathrm{p}}}$ the antiproton needs to travel from $\mathrm{S}_1$ to $\mathrm{S}_2$. If a $\pi^{-}$ meson has the same kinetic energy as the antiproton, find the time $t_{\pi^{-}}$ the $\pi^{-}$ meson needs to travel from $\mathrm{S}_1$ to $\mathrm{S}_2$.

(2) A charged particle moving with speed $v$ ($v>c/n$) passes through a medium of refractive index $n$. Find the angle $\theta$ between the propagation direction of the Cherenkov radiation produced and the direction of motion of the charged particle.

(3) A differential Cherenkov counter can record the number of particles with speeds in a certain interval. Figure 6b is the schematic cross-section of such a counter, which is rotationally symmetric about its axis (the dashed line in the figure). The light collection system consists of a spherical mirror of radius $R$ and an annular diaphragm of adjustable radius. When the angle $\theta$ between the propagation direction of the Cherenkov radiation and the direction of motion of the charged particle is very small, the spherical mirror focuses the Cherenkov radiation excited by the charged particle onto its focal plane, forming a ring of radiation of radius $r$, which is projected onto the counters. For the radiation excited by a charged particle of speed $v$, find the radius of the ring of light.

The difference between the total kinetic energy of the particles in the final state of the reaction and the total kinetic energy of the particles in the initial state is the reaction energy $Q$. As shown in Figure 6c, the Dalitz plot is an equilateral triangle of height 1, and the distances from a point P to the three sides equal the fractions of the reaction energy carried as kinetic energy by the three $\pi^{0}$ mesons, i.e. $d_i=E_{k,i}/Q$, where $E_{k,i}$ is the kinetic energy of the $i$-th $\pi^{0}$ meson, $i=1,2,3$. Find the expression for the boundary of the region in which the point P may lie, in terms of the reaction energy $Q$, the $\pi^{0}$ meson mass $m_{\pi^{0}}$ and the speed of light in vacuum $c$. Also discuss the expression for the boundary of the region of the point P if $m_{\pi^{0}}=0$.

Problem 1

[40 points] The smooth running of a high-speed train is closely related to the degree of vibration of the train; air springs installed on the train can effectively damp vibrations. The air-spring model used in a certain high-speed-train test experiment consists of a main air chamber (an air bag) and an auxiliary air chamber (of constant volume), as shown in Figure 1a. The vertically upward force exerted by the air spring on the sprung load is provided by the elastic force produced by the compressed air inside the air bag. When the sprung load is in equilibrium, the pressure and volume of the gas in the main air chamber are $p_{10}$ and $V_{10}$ respectively, the volume of the auxiliary air chamber is $V_2$, and the atmospheric pressure is $p_0$. The ratio of the vertically upward force $F$ of the air spring to the difference between the pressure of the gas in the main air chamber and the atmospheric pressure is called the effective bearing area $A_{\mathrm{e}}$ of the air spring. The molar heat capacity of air at constant volume is known to be $C_V = \frac{5}{2}R$ ($R$ is the universal gas constant). Assume that, under small-amplitude vibration, both the volume $V_1$ of the gas in the main air chamber and the effective bearing area $A_{\mathrm{e}}$ can be regarded as linear functions of the vertical displacement $y$ (positive downward) of the bearing surface of the air spring (air bag) relative to its equilibrium position, with rates of change equal to the constants $-\alpha$ ($\alpha > 0$) and $\beta$ ($\beta > 0$) respectively.

(1) With the auxiliary air chamber not connected to the main air chamber (valve closed), derive, in each of the following two cases, the relation between the stiffness $K \equiv \mathrm{d}F/\mathrm{d}y$ of the air spring and its effective bearing area $A_{\mathrm{e}}$:

i) passengers getting on and off (the changes of pressure and volume of the gas in the main air chamber follow an isothermal process);

ii) the train meets violent jolting while running (the changes of pressure and volume of the gas in the main air chamber follow an adiabatic process).

(2) With the main air chamber connected to the auxiliary air chamber (valve open), derive, in the two cases above, the relation between the stiffness $K$ of the air spring and its effective bearing area $A_{\mathrm{e}}$. Problem 2

[40 points] A homogeneous solid cue ball of mass $m$ and radius $R$ rests on a horizontal table; the coefficient of sliding friction between the cue ball and the table is $\mu$. The cue is adjusted so that it lies horizontally in the vertical plane through the centre of the ball, and it strikes the upper half of the cue ball; the height of the cue relative to the horizontal plane containing the centre of the ball is $R/2$, and the duration of the strike is extremely short. The impulse received by the cue ball has magnitude $P$ and is horizontal. Assume that the maximum static friction force equals the sliding friction force. The magnitude of the gravitational acceleration is $g$.

(1) How long after the strike does the cue ball begin pure rolling? Find the velocity of the centre of the ball when the cue ball reaches pure rolling.

(2) Let B be the point of the cue ball in contact with the table at the moment when the cue ball reaches pure rolling (take this moment as the zero of time). Find the position, velocity and acceleration of the point B on the ball at a subsequent time $t'$.

Problem 3

[40 points] The negative differential resistance effect is the property of certain circuits or electronic components (such as the tunnel diode) that, within a particular voltage range, their current decreases as the terminal voltage increases; this effect can sustain high-frequency oscillations in a circuit and output an amplified AC signal. In the simplified circuit shown in Figure 3a, D is a tunnel diode. On its left side there is a fixed resistor $R$, an inductor $L$ and a capacitor $C$ connected in series; the AC current in this loop is denoted by $i(t)$. On its right side there is an ideal high-frequency choke RFC (zero DC resistance, completely blocking AC signals) and an ideal constant-voltage DC source $V_0$; the DC current in this loop is denoted by $I$ ($I \gg |i(t)|$). The positive directions of the currents are marked in the figure. D always stays within the particular voltage range, in which its resistance is $-R_0$ ($R_0 > 0$, and is a constant).

$$i(t) = \alpha_1 e^{\beta_1 t} + \alpha_2 e^{\beta_2 t}, \quad (\alpha_1,\ \beta_1,\ \alpha_2,\ \beta_2 \text{ are constants to be determined})$$

Determine the constants $\alpha_1$, $\beta_1$, $\alpha_2$, $\beta_2$, so as to determine the AC current $i(t)$ at any time $t$.

(2) Explain under what condition resonance (harmonic oscillation) occurs in the left loop. Find the current $i_{\mathrm{H}}(t)$ in the left loop and the resonance frequency $f_{\mathrm{H}}$ in the case of resonance.

(4) It is known that the range in which the tunnel diode D works normally (i.e. keeps its negative differential resistance effect) is

Find the maximum average power $\bar{P}_{\max}$ that the AC part on the tunnel diode can reach, and the output voltage $V_0$ of the ideal constant-voltage DC source in that case.
